_readme: Point2Rem — 'points to remember'. Free-form notes carrying ::-hierarchical
tags and optional links to existing AdsHub problems. Rendered by the
AdsHub sidebar's Point2Rem tab (grouped by tag, tree or flat); selecting an
item opens it in the right-hand detail pane.
THIS FILE IS ONLY A SEED. The live notes are rows in the 'Point2Rem' tab of
the Google Sheet, created + edited from the portal (＋ New / ✎ / 🗑). This
file is copied into that tab once, when the tab is first created; editing it
afterwards changes nothing for a sheet that already exists.
id        required, unique, kebab-case — used for selection + deep links
title     required, shown in the list and the detail header
content   markdown by default; set format:'html' to write raw HTML
problems  LC frontend ids — rendered as clickable rows that open the
updated   free-form date string, shown in the detail header

items.title: Two pointers: name the invariant before you move one
items.content:
Every two-pointer solution is really *one sentence* about what stays true between `lo` and `hi`. Write it down first — the move rule then falls out of it.

- **Sorted pair sum** — invariant: *the answer, if it exists, is inside `[lo, hi]`*. `sum < target` ⇒ `lo++` (no smaller left can help), `sum > target` ⇒ `hi--`.
- **Container with most water** — invariant: *the taller wall can never be the limiting one for any narrower window*. So always move the **shorter** wall.
- **3Sum** — sort, fix `i`, then it degenerates to the sorted pair sum. The only real work is de-duplicating `i` and both pointers.

If you can't state the invariant in one line, you're pattern-matching, not solving.

items.title: Sliding window: the shrink condition is the whole problem
items.content:
The expand step is always the same (`right++`, update counts). All the variation lives in **when you shrink**:

| Question shape | Shrink while… | Record answer |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Longest valid window | window is **invalid** | after shrinking |
| Shortest valid window | window is **valid** | before shrinking |
| Exactly K distinct | `atMost(K) - atMost(K-1)` | — |

The "exactly K" trick is worth memorising: almost nobody writes a correct direct version under time pressure, and the `atMost` decomposition is three lines of reuse.

items.title: Grid traversal: pick BFS or DFS by what the answer measures
items.content:
- Answer is a **count / area / connectivity** ⇒ DFS is fine (and shorter).
- Answer is a **distance or a number of steps** ⇒ BFS, because the first time you touch a cell is already the shortest way there.
- Several sources spread at once (rotting oranges, nearest-zero) ⇒ **multi-source BFS**: push *all* sources into the queue before the first pop. This is the single highest-leverage grid trick — it turns an O(n²) per-source loop into one sweep.
- Reachability *from* the border inward (Pacific/Atlantic) ⇒ invert the question and flood **from** the edges.

items.title: DP: state, transition, base, order — in that order
items.content:
Before writing a single loop, answer four questions on paper:

1. **State** — what does `dp[i]` (or `dp[i][j]`) *mean* in English? If the sentence needs an "and also", the state is under-specified.
2. **Transition** — which earlier states can reach it, and at what cost?
3. **Base case** — the smallest state whose value you know without computing.
4. **Order** — an iteration order in which every dependency is already filled.

Most "my DP is off by one" bugs are really a step-1 problem: `dp[i]` meaning *"using the first i items"* vs *"ending exactly at i"* leads to two different answers, and mixing them mid-solution is the classic failure.

items.title: Heaps: keep the heap the size of the answer, not the input
items.content:
For "top K of N", the reflex is a max-heap of all N. The better move is a **min-heap capped at K**: push, and pop when `size > K`. O(N log K) time, O(K) space, and the heap root is the answer boundary at every moment.

Mirror rule: for "K largest" use a **min**-heap; for "K smallest" use a **max**-heap. Getting this backwards is the most common heap bug, and it fails silently on small inputs.

items.title: Interview: five clarifying questions that always pay
items.content:
Cheap to ask, expensive to assume:

1. Input size — decides whether O(n²) is acceptable or disqualifying.
2. Value range / negatives — kills or enables counting-sort, prefix sums, two pointers on a sorted array.
3. Duplicates — changes the de-dup work and sometimes the whole return type.
4. Return shape — the value, the indices, or the count? These are three different solutions.
5. Mutability of the input — permission to sort in place is often the entire optimisation.

Asking these takes ninety seconds and routinely saves ten minutes of rewriting.

items.title: A valid tree is more than “no cycle”
items.content:
For `n` nodes:

```
valid tree  ⇔  connected  AND  no cycle
            ⇔  connected  AND  exactly n - 1 edges
```

So either **detect a cycle and check there's one component**, or take the `n - 1` edges shortcut.

The edge-count line is the cheap guard: with fewer than `n - 1` edges it can't be connected, with more it must contain a cycle. Check `edges.length === n - 1` first, then a single traversal from node `0` only has to prove it reaches all `n` nodes — no separate cycle check needed.

The half-answer to avoid: "no cycle ⇒ tree". A forest of two acyclic components passes that test and is not a tree.

items.title: Undirected cycle ≠ “neighbour already seen” — it's the parent
items.content:
In an undirected edge `{u, v}`, going `u → v` puts `u` in `v`'s neighbour list, already visited. That is **not** a cycle — it's the edge you arrived on.

```
visited neighbour == parent  → OK (the edge you came on)
visited neighbour != parent  → cycle
```

Same rule for BFS and DFS: carry the parent alongside each node (`stack.push([next, node])` / `queue.push([next, node])`) and skip only that one.

Two traps the parent check alone doesn't cover:

- **Parallel edges** — `{u, v}` listed twice is a genuine cycle, but the second copy looks exactly like the parent. Track visited *edges* if the input allows duplicates.
- **Self-loops** — `{u, u}` is a cycle; the parent test happily lets it through.

In a directed graph none of this applies: there, a cycle means the neighbour is on the current recursion stack, not merely visited.

items.title: O(n·m) brute force: name what the inner loop recomputes, then pick the store
items.content:
When two strings or arrays give `O(n·k)` / `O(n·m)` brute force, the inner loop is **re-comparing (or re-deriving) something it already knew**. Don't hunt for a cleverer loop. Name the recompute, then **pick a store from the solutions-tool menu** — pay once in space for what the loop keeps re-deriving.

The menu is the pattern to remember. Prefix-sum, DP, a couple of swapped variables — those are *rows on the same menu*, not three unrelated tricks.

Three questions, in order:

1. **What does the inner loop recompute?** A range sum, a window-vs-pattern comparison, a subproblem, "have I seen this"…
2. **Does that thing depend on only *one* of the two inputs — or only on data already seen?** If yes, hoist it out and compute it once. That is the whole trick.
3. **How big is the key space?** That picks the row.

| Inner loop recomputes… | Store to pick | Anchors |
| --- | --- | --- |
| a sum / count over a range | prefix-sum (prefix-count) array | 303, 560 |
| the same subproblem with the same args | memo / DP table | 1143, 322 |
| a DP row that only looks back 1–2 cells | two variables, rolled + swapped | 53, 121 |
| "have I seen value X before?" | hash set / map value → index | 1, 560 |
| max / min over a moving window | monotonic deque | 239, 84 |
| comparing a window to a fixed pattern | rolling hash of the window | 1044, 28 |
| how far to shift a pattern after a mismatch | LPS / failure table over the **pattern** | 28, 459, 214 |

Sizing shortcut: O(1) state ⇒ **variables** you swap; keyed by index ⇒ **array**; keyed by value ⇒ **hash**; keyed by `(i, j)` ⇒ **table**.

strStr (28) is the last two rows — same bottleneck, two stores. Worked derivation of why the store is LPS (not prefix-sum, not a DP table over both strings): *strStr: a mismatch teaches you about the needle*.

items.title: strStr: a mismatch teaches you about the needle, not the haystack
items.content:
Pattern · LPS / KMP fall-back · not a strStr write-up
Preprocess the pattern’s self-overlap. On mismatch jump j, never i.
1 Brute restartmismatch → r+1, j = 0 · O(n·m)
→
2 Name the recomputesame chars re-read up to m times
→
3 Store LPS on the patternO(m) table · not the text
→
4 j = lps[j−1]i only moves forward · O(n+m)
Remember
Bottleneck: restarting from j = 0 re-reads the text → O(n·m).
Don’t invent a loop. Pick the store: lps on the pattern.
lps[k] = longest proper prefix that is also a suffix of p[:k+1].
On mismatch: leave i (text) · set j = lps[j-1] (pattern).
i never goes backward ⇒ O(n+m) (same amortised idea as sliding-window left).
lps[-1] alone is often the whole answer (period / happy prefix / palindrome prefix).
Visual · mismatch jumps j, not i
i · text (stays) j · pattern (jumps) lps overlap mismatch
p / lps abab index 0 1 2 3 · lps 0 0 1 2
text abaX
pattern abab mismatch at j = 3
↓ lps[2] = 1 → j = 1 · i stays
text abaX
pattern   ab trailing “a” was already a prefix · resume at needle[1]
Why the store is the pattern
After j matches: text[i-j : i] == p[:j]. So “where can I restart?” is only:
which suffix of p[:j] is also a prefix of p?
The text has left the question → compute once, reuse on every scan.
One skeleton
def build_lps(p):
    lps, k = [0] * len(p), 0
    for i in range(1, len(p)):
        while k and p[i] != p[k]:
            k = lps[k - 1]          # fall back on the pattern
        if p[i] == p[k]: k += 1
        lps[i] = k
    return lps

j = 0
for i, ch in enumerate(text):          # never rewind i
    while j and ch != p[j]:
        j = lps[j - 1]
    if ch == p[j]: j += 1
    if j == len(p):
        # hit at i-j+1; for all hits: j = lps[j-1]
        ...
Same pattern · other problems

The move is identical. Only the readout of lps changes.

AskReadout
find pattern in textscan skeleton · 28, 686, 1408, 796
longest prefix that is also a suffixlps[-1] is the answer · 1392
is s a repeat of a smaller blocklps[-1] > 0 and n % (n - lps[-1]) == 0 · 459
shortest palindrome by prependingLPS of s + '#' + s[::-1]; lps[-1] = palindrome prefix · 214
459   s = a b c a b c a b c   n = 9
lps[-1] = 6 → period = n − 6 = 3 (“abc”)   ·   9 % 3 == 0 ✓
214   s + '#' + reverse(s) = a a c # c a a
lps[-1] = 2 → “aa” is already a palindrome prefix   ·   prepend reverse(“c”) → caac

Sister store on the same bottleneck: rolling-hash the window (Rabin-Karp) — fingerprint the text instead of storing structure inside the pattern.

items.title: 2D → 1D DP: the row array changes identity as you sweep it
items.content:
The whole idea in one line. The 2D table is only ever read one row back. Everything older is dead weight — so keep one row and let it change identity as you sweep across it.

1 · Find what the transition actually reads

Before touching the code, write the dependency down. For Unique Paths:

ways[r][c] = ways[r-1][c] + ways[r][c-1]
             ↑ row above   ↑ same row, one left
  • up = previous row, same column → in 1D that's row[c] before you overwrite it
  • left = current row, previous column → row[c-1], already overwritten this sweep

No index goes back further than one row. That single fact is the whole licence to drop a dimension.

2 · The overwrite moment — the only thing to really understand

One slot, row[c], means two different things depending on when you read it:
before the assignmentways[r-1][c] — the row above (up)
after the assignmentways[r][c] — the current row

The array is half old row, half new row mid-sweep: everything left of c is already the new row, everything from c rightward is still the old one. Your up = row[c] line is exactly the act of grabbing the old value before it's clobbered.

3 · Your two versions, lined up

# 2D — push style, m×n memory
ways = [[0] * n for _ in range(m)]
ways[0][0] = 1
for r in range(m):
    for c in range(n):
        for tr, tc in [(1,0), (0,1)]:
            nr, nc = r+tr, c+tc
            if nr < m and nc < n:
                ways[nr][nc] += ways[r][c]
return ways[m-1][n-1]
# 1D — one row of memory
row = [1] * n                 # row 0: exactly one way to each cell
for r in range(1, m):
    left = 1                  # column 0 is always 1
    for c in range(1, n):
        up   = row[c]         # OLD row — grab before clobbering
        row[c] = up + left    # slot flips to the new row here
        left = row[c]         # carry rightward
return row[n-1]
Once you see it, left is redundant. After row[c-1] was assigned it already is the current row's left neighbour — so the loop body collapses to one line: 
row = [1] * n
for _ in range(1, m):
    for c in range(1, n):
        row[c] += row[c-1]    # up (old row[c]) + left (new row[c-1])
return row[n-1]
Verified: 2D, your 1D, and this form all equal C(m+n−2, m−1) for every m,n ≤ 8.

4 · The sweep direction is a rule, not a guess

Direction decides which version of a slot you read. Pick it from what the transition needs:

Transition readsSweepBecause
dp[r][c-1] — current row, leftforward →you want the already-updated value
dp[r-1][c-1] — old row, left (diagonal)forward + stashthat slot is already destroyed — save it first
dp[r-1][c-w] — old row, far left (0/1 knapsack)backward ←going forward would reuse the item twice

5 · The diagonal case — where 1D actually bites

LCS / edit distance need dp[i-1][j-1]. By the time you reach j, row[j-1] is the new row — reading it as the diagonal is silently wrong, not crashy.
Measured: dropping the stash gives a wrong LCS on 603 of 2000 random string pairs — it passes small examples often enough to look right.
def lcs(a, b):
    row = [0] * (len(b) + 1)
    for ca in a:
        prev = 0                  # dp[i-1][j-1] for j = 0
        for j, cb in enumerate(b, 1):
            cur = row[j]          # save dp[i-1][j] BEFORE overwrite
            row[j] = prev + 1 if ca == cb else max(row[j], row[j-1])
            prev = cur            # it's the diagonal for the next j
    return row[-1]

Verified against the 2D table over 2000 random pairs.

6 · Knapsack: direction is the semantics

for w, v in zip(weights, values):
    for c in range(cap, w-1, -1):   # DESC → each item used once (0/1)
        dp[c] = max(dp[c], dp[c-w] + v)

    for c in range(w, cap+1):       # ASC → item reusable (unbounded)
        dp[c] = max(dp[c], dp[c-w] + v)

Same body, one word different, two different problems. Ascending answers 0/1 wrongly on 272 of 400 random instances — because dp[c-w] already includes this item.

7 · The mechanical checklist

  1. Write the transition and list every index it reads.
  2. Is the deepest read r-1? Yes → one row is enough. r-2 → keep two rows. Arbitrary r' → don't reduce.
  3. Reads only current-row-left → sweep forward, done.
  4. Reads the diagonal → sweep forward, stash the pre-overwrite value in prev.
  5. Reads old-row-left at distance w → sweep backward.
  6. Base case: the 2D first row becomes the array's initial contents.
When NOT to reduce. If you must reconstruct the path (which edits, which items), keep the 2D table — the backtrack needs the history you just threw away. Space reduction is for when only the final number matters. In an interview: write the 2D, get it correct, then say "this only reads one row back, so it collapses to O(n) space" — and reduce if asked.

items.title: Grid: three memory models — visited kind changes the count
items.content:
Matrix · grid memory · not Unique Paths specifically
Different kind of visited → the counting method changes completely. Pick the memory model from the question, not from the islands template.
Three memory models · three questions
Global visited
seen set · never un-marked
  • Asks: was this cell ever reached?
  • Fits: reachability, shortest path
  • Cost: linear · BFS / flood DFS
  • 200, 542, 994
Count per cell
ways[r][c] · no visited
  • Asks: how many ways to arrive here?
  • Fits: moves never go back — the grid is a DAG
  • Cost: polynomial · DP
  • 62, 63, 64
Path-local visited
mark → recurse → un-mark
  • Asks: have I used this cell on the current path?
  • Fits: moves can loop — count simple paths
  • Cost: exponential · backtracking
  • 79, 980
DAG — Directed Acyclic Graph. Arrows only; no way to come back to where you were. Down/right (or any strictly increasing index) is a DAG. Four directions is not.
Why DP breaks the moment you allow 4 directions
  • ways[r][c] = ways[above] + ways[left] works because above and left are always finished first.
  • With 4 directions, ways[r][c] depends on ways[r][c+1], which depends on ways[r][c] again. Circular. No fill order.
  • Worse: without a visited rule the answer is infinite — the robot can walk a loop forever.
4-direction visited must be per-path

Not a global set. Mark on the way in, un-mark on the way out. That is backtracking.

def count_simple_paths(m, n):
    on_path = [[False] * n for _ in range(m)]

    def dfs(r, c):
        if (r, c) == (m-1, n-1):
            return 1
        on_path[r][c] = True               # mark: this path is using the cell
        total = 0
        for dr, dc in [(1,0), (0,1), (-1,0), (0,-1)]:
            nr, nc = r+dr, c+dc
            if 0 <= nr < m and 0 <= nc < n and not on_path[nr][nc]:
                total += dfs(nr, nc)
        on_path[r][c] = False              # un-mark: other paths may still use it
        return total

    return dfs(0, 0)
The un-mark line is the whole difference from the islands template. Other paths may still use this cell. Only this path may not use it twice.
No clever table here. Counting simple paths in a general graph is hard. Cost is exponential in the grid size.
Analogy · chalk vs rope
Global visited = chalk on the door
  • Once marked, nobody enters again.
  • Good for “which rooms exist” / shortest first visit.
Per-path visited = a rope you drag
  • You can’t step on your own rope.
  • Back out, coil it up → the next explorer can walk there freely.
Rule of thumb · decide the memory model
1 Can a move bring me back?toward where I came from
→
N No visited · DPdown/right · strictly increasing · polynomial
→
Y Visited is requiredthen ask what you are counting
If yes, counting cells / reachability / shortest distance
  • Global visited · never un-mark
  • BFS / DFS · linear
If yes, counting distinct paths
  • Per-path visited with un-marking
  • Backtracking · exponential
4 directions needs a visited record — a per-path one, not the global one from the islands template.
